description: Black Tudors, John Blanke, Lascar seamen and the East India Company's Asian connections.
content_html:
Africans in Early Modern England

The presence of African people in England long predates the transatlantic slave trade. Tudor-era records, analysed by historians Miranda Kaufmann and Onyeka Nubia, document Black individuals living and working across England from the early sixteenth century. They arrived through several routes: as members of Spanish and Portuguese diplomatic parties, as servants brought by merchants, and as skilled professionals in their own right.

The most vividly documented African Tudor was John Blanke, who served as a royal trumpeter at the courts of Henry VII and Henry VIII. He is depicted in the Westminster Tournament Roll of 1511 — a colourful contemporary illustration that shows him mounted on horseback alongside other royal musicians. Blanke was not enslaved; he received a royal wage and petitioned Henry VIII for a pay rise, which was granted. His story challenges any assumption that Africans in Tudor England were automatically enslaved or marginalised.

Other documented individuals include Reasonable Blackman, a Southwark silk-weaver active around 1507, who appears in London parish records as an independent craftsman. Church baptism, marriage and burial records across London, Bristol and Plymouth record dozens of African individuals between 1500 and 1600. Historian Miranda Kaufmann has traced the lives of over 360 Black Tudors in the archives.

Key Fact

In 1596 and again in 1601, Elizabeth I issued proclamations about the presence of “blackamoors” in England — expressing displeasure at their numbers and ordering that some be deported. However, historians note that these proclamations had little practical effect: there is no evidence of organised deportations, and Africans continued to live and work in England. The proclamations tell us about royal attitudes but do not accurately describe what happened to Black people in Tudor England.

Medieval Aliens: Resident Strangers in England

Before the Tudor period, England’s towns had hosted significant communities of foreign merchants and craftspeople throughout the Middle Ages. Alien residents paid special taxes (the “alien subsidy”), faced restrictions on trading independently, and were sometimes required to live with English hosts. Flemish weavers brought advanced textile techniques to East Anglia and Kent. Italian merchants from Florence, Genoa and Venice dominated the luxury trade through London’s Lombard Street. German merchants of the Hanseatic League operated from the Steelyard, a privileged enclave in London, from the thirteenth century until Henry VIII curtailed their privileges in the 1520s.

These communities created periodic tensions with native English merchants, who complained that alien traders undercut local prices and took trade away from English guilds. But they also drove economic growth, introduced new skills, and helped integrate England into wider European commercial networks.

The East India Company, chartered by Elizabeth I on 31 December 1600, opened sustained commercial connections between England and South Asia. These connections produced an early flow of South Asian people to Britain. Among the first were Lascar seamen — sailors recruited in Bengal and other Indian coastal regions to crew East India Company ships. Because the Company rotated its ships through English ports, Lascars regularly arrived in London, Bristol and other ports. Some were stranded when contracts ended and their ships departed, forming small South Asian communities in port districts.

South Asian servants also arrived in England from the late seventeenth century onwards. Wealthy East India Company officials and merchants brought Indian servants, particularly women employed as nursemaids or “ayahs.” Child servants from India appeared in English household records. These individuals occupied marginal and often vulnerable positions, dependent on their employers and without legal protections. Some were abandoned when their employers returned to India or died.

Key Fact

John Lok brought five Africans to London in 1555 as part of a trading expedition to West Africa. This is one of the earliest documented cases of Africans being brought to England specifically as part of the Atlantic commercial system. Lok intended to teach them English so they could serve as interpreters for future trading voyages — a reminder that the early African presence in England was bound up with commercial expansion, not only with later slavery.

The lives of African and Asian migrants in early modern England were diverse. John Blanke’s story — a salaried royal musician who petitioned for better pay — demonstrates that some Black individuals in Tudor England were skilled professionals with recognised standing. Reasonable Blackman’s presence as an independent craftsman in London shows integration into the artisan economy. At the same time, the later development of chattel slavery in the Atlantic meant that by the late seventeenth century, the position of enslaved Africans brought to England by returning colonists was very different from that of the free Black Tudors.

Historians caution against two oversimplifications: celebrating Tudor diversity anachronistically as if racism did not exist, and assuming that all Africans in early modern England were enslaved. The documentary evidence demands a more nuanced reading. These were individuals with names, occupations, families and, in some cases, the capacity to act as agents in their own lives.
exam_tip_html: This lesson spans two broad periods (medieval ‘aliens’ and early modern African/Asian arrivals), so be careful to use evidence from the correct period when answering questions. For “Describe Two Features” questions about Africans in Tudor England, give specific named examples — John Blanke and Reasonable Blackman are better evidence than vague statements about “some Africans”. For longer essays, note that both communities (medieval alien merchants and Tudor Africans) illustrate the recurring pattern of economic utility shaping reception: they were welcome when economically useful and faced hostility when their role was questioned or threatened.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • African people were present in Tudor England as free individuals with documented occupations: John Blanke served as a royal trumpeter at the courts of Henry VII and Henry VIII, and Reasonable Blackman worked as a Southwark silk-weaver — both were free and active participants in English society.
  • Medieval England hosted substantial communities of alien merchants — Flemish weavers, Italian bankers and German Hanseatic traders — who contributed to economic growth but also faced restrictions and periodic resentment from English guilds.
  • The chartering of the East India Company in 1600 opened sustained South Asian connections to England: Lascar seamen and South Asian servants arrived in port cities from the late seventeenth century, forming the earliest South Asian communities in Britain.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the African presence in Tudor England.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: Africans lived as free individuals in Tudor England (1); for example, John Blanke was a royal trumpeter who received wages and petitioned for a pay rise from Henry VIII (1). Feature 2: Africans worked in a range of skilled occupations (1); Reasonable Blackman was an independent silk-weaver in Southwark, documented in London parish records (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why South Asian people began arriving in England from the seventeenth century onwards.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two reasons fully developed with specific evidence. Reason 1: The East India Company (chartered 1600) recruited Lascar seamen from Bengal and other coastal regions; as ships rotated through English ports, some sailors remained and formed communities in port districts. Reason 2: East India Company officials returning to England brought South Asian servants — ayahs (nursemaids) and other domestic workers — who were sometimes abandoned on arrival and formed vulnerable migrant communities. Secure: Both reasons explained with evidence. Developing: One reason explained well. Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which alien residents in medieval England contributed to the economy.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Examples: Flemish weavers brought advanced textile techniques to East Anglia and Kent (1), driving growth in the English cloth industry (1); Hanseatic League merchants operated from the Steelyard in London (1), integrating England into European trading networks (1); Italian merchants from Florence and Genoa dominated luxury goods trade through Lombard Street (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the experiences of African individuals in Tudor England varied so widely.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies that diversity of experience reflected diversity of legal status and occupation — John Blanke was a salaried professional with standing; Reasonable Blackman an independent craftsman; later enslaved Africans brought by colonists had no legal protections. Connects this to the development of Atlantic slavery as a distinct system from the earlier presence of free African individuals. Secure: Explains variation with at least two specific contrasting examples. Developing: Notes some variation with limited evidence. Emerging: Descriptive account without explanation.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that African migrants in early modern England were primarily victims of racial discrimination? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that balances evidence of agency (John Blanke, Reasonable Blackman, John Lok's interpreters) against evidence of discrimination (Elizabeth I's proclamations, later development of slavery, vulnerability of Lascars and ayahs); engages with Miranda Kaufmann and Onyeka Nubia's historical research; avoids both uncritical celebration and flattening all experiences as victimhood. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from both sides. Developing: Some awareness of complexity with basic evidence. Emerging: Descriptive. SPaG: 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the chartering of the East India Company in 1600 led to new patterns of migration to England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two patterns explained with specific causal links — Lascar seamen recruited in India arrived in English ports and sometimes settled when stranded; South Asian domestic workers brought back by Company officials formed vulnerable communities. Explains how the Company's commercial operations directly caused these movements. Secure: Two patterns explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One pattern explained. Emerging: General statements about trade and migration.

flashcard_questions.a: African trumpeter at the courts of Henry VII and Henry VIII, depicted in the 1511 Westminster Tournament Roll
Independent silk-weaver in Southwark, documented in London parish records around 1507
South Asian sailors recruited by the East India Company, who often arrived in English ports from the 1660s onwards
South Asian nursemaids or female servants brought to England by East India Company officials

flashcard_questions.q: What did Elizabeth I's proclamations of 1596 and 1601 concern?
flashcard_questions.a: The presence of 'blackamoors' in England — though the proclamations had little practical effect

flashcard_questions.q: When was the East India Company chartered?
Name one medieval alien community that contributed to the English economy.
flashcard_questions.a: Flemish weavers (textiles), Italian merchants (finance/luxury goods), or Hanseatic League traders (European trade)

flashcard_questions.q: What does historian Miranda Kaufmann's research reveal about Black Tudors?
flashcard_questions.a: She traced over 360 Black individuals in Tudor archives — most were free, not enslaved

glossary_terms.definition: African trumpeter in the courts of Henry VII and Henry VIII, depicted in the 1511 Westminster Tournament Roll — one of the few Africans in Tudor England whose face and name are both known.
Foreign residents in medieval and early modern England who did not hold the full legal rights of English subjects and were subject to additional taxes and restrictions.
A network of north German trading cities whose merchants operated from the Steelyard in London, a privileged trading post active from the thirteenth to the sixteenth century.
A joint-stock trading company chartered by Elizabeth I in 1600 to conduct trade with Asia, which became the engine of British commercial expansion into India and South-East Asia.
South Asian sailors employed on British merchant and naval vessels from the seventeenth century onwards, many of whom were recruited in Bengal and other coastal regions of India.
